rate-laws-s1.title: Initial rates for making nitrosyl chloride
rate-laws-s1.text:
Nitrogen monoxide and chlorine react at a fixed temperature:

2 NO(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 NOCl(g)

Three trials start with different concentrations, and the initial rate of formation of NOCl is measured in each.

rate-laws-s2.title: A reaction that ignores one reactant
rate-laws-s2.text: Two dissolved reactants, X and Y, react at 25 °C. Initial rates of disappearance of X are measured.

table.caption: Initial concentrations and rates for X + Y → products

items.q: What is the order of the reaction with respect to NO?
options: Zero order
First order
Second order
Third order

why.correct: Compare trials 1 and 2, where only [NO] changes: [NO] doubles and the rate goes from 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ to 7.20 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, a factor of 4. Since 2ᵐ = 4, m = 2.
options: Zero order would leave the rate unchanged when [NO] changes.
First order would double the rate when [NO] doubles; here it quadruples.
Right: doubling [NO] multiplies the rate by 4 = 2².
Third order would multiply the rate by 2³ = 8.

items.q: What is the order of the reaction with respect to Cl₂?
options: Zero order
Half order
First order
Second order

why.correct: Compare trials 1 and 3, where only [Cl₂] changes: it doubles and the rate doubles (1.80 → 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ M/s). 2ⁿ = 2 gives n = 1.
options: Zero order would leave the rate unchanged; it doubled.
Half order would multiply the rate by about 1.4, not 2.
Right: the rate changes by the same factor as [Cl₂].
Second order would quadruple the rate when [Cl₂] doubles.

items.q: Using trial 1, calculate the rate constant k. Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you used [NO] to the first power. The rate law is second order in NO, so square it: (0.0100 M)².
Value: no factor of 2 belongs here. The rate law and k come from the measured rate directly, not from the coefficient of NOCl.

why.correct: rate = k[NO]²[Cl₂], so k = rate / ([NO]²[Cl₂]) = (1.80 × 10⁻⁴ M/s) / ((0.0100 M)²(0.0100 M)) = (1.80 × 10⁻⁴ M/s) / (1.00 × 10⁻⁶ M³) = 1.80 × 10² M⁻² s⁻¹. The units are M/s ÷ M³ = M⁻² s⁻¹.

items.q: Predict the initial rate, in M/s, of a fourth trial with [NO] = 0.0300 M and [Cl₂] = 0.0050 M.

mistakes.why: Value: [NO] must be squared. The rate law is second order in NO.
Value: tripling [NO] multiplies the rate by 3² = 9, not 3.

why.correct: rate = k[NO]²[Cl₂] = (180 M⁻² s⁻¹)(0.0300 M)²(0.0050 M) = (180)(9.00 × 10⁻⁴)(0.0050) M/s = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. By ratios: [NO] ×3 gives ×9, [Cl₂] ×½ gives ×½, and 1.80 × 10⁻⁴ × 4.5 = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. Two significant figures, from 0.0050 M.

items.q: A student says, "The coefficient of NO is 2 and of Cl₂ is 1, so I could have written the rate law without doing the experiment." Which response is best?
options: Orders come from data; here they happen to match the coefficients
The student is right: rate-law orders are the coefficients of the balanced equation
The orders match the coefficients of the products, not those of the reactants
For gas reactions like this one, coefficients give the orders

why.correct: The balanced equation shows how much reacts in total, not how the rate depends on each concentration. Here the measured orders (2 and 1) happen to equal the coefficients; for many reactions they do not, so the orders must come from experiment.
options: Right: orders are measured; a match with coefficients is a coincidence for an overall equation.
This is the misconception: the overall equation does not tell you the orders.
Product coefficients do not set the orders either; orders are found by experiment.
Being gases makes no difference; orders still come from data.

items.q: Which rate law agrees with the data?
options: rate = k[X]
rate = k[X][Y]
rate = k[Y]
rate = k[X]²

why.correct: Trials 1 and 2: [X] doubles, rate doubles, so first order in X. Trials 1 and 3: [Y] triples, rate is unchanged, so zero order in Y ([Y]⁰ = 1). rate = k[X].
options: Right: first order in X, zero order in Y.
Tripling [Y] would triple the rate; the data show no change.
The rate does not change with [Y] but does change with [X].
Doubling [X] would quadruple the rate; it only doubles.

items.q: Y is still used up as the reaction goes. Which statement about Y is consistent with the data?
options: Y is used up, but its concentration does not set the rate
Y is not consumed by the reaction
Y is a product of the reaction, not a reactant
Y is a solid, so it has no concentration

why.correct: Zero order in Y means changing [Y] does not change the rate. Y can still be consumed; it simply is not involved in whatever controls the speed (topic 5.8 explains how a mechanism can leave a reactant out of the rate law).
options: Right: zero order means the rate does not depend on [Y], not that Y is not used.
Y is listed as a reactant and is consumed; zero order only means its concentration does not set the rate.
Y is on the reactant side of the equation.
The stem says Y is dissolved; its concentration was varied from 0.15 M to 0.45 M.

items.q: Using the data for X, what is the first-order rate constant? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by [X][Y]. The rate law is rate = k[X], so divide by [X] only.

why.correct: k = rate / [X] = (2.4 × 10⁻⁵ M/s) / (0.15 M) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. For a first-order rate law the units are M/s ÷ M = s⁻¹.

items.q: Predict the initial rate, in M/s, when [X] = 0.45 M and [Y] = 0.30 M.

mistakes.why: Value: [Y] does not appear in the rate law, so doubling [Y] does not change the rate.

why.correct: rate = k[X] = (1.6 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹)(0.45 M) = 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ M/s. [Y] is zero order, so its value does not matter.

items.q: For rate = k[A][B]², what are the units of k when concentrations are in M and time in s?
options: M s⁻¹
s⁻¹
M⁻¹ s⁻¹
M⁻² s⁻¹

why.correct: The overall order is 1 + 2 = 3. k = rate/([A][B]²) has units (M/s)/M³ = M⁻² s⁻¹.
options: These are the units of a rate, which is also the units of k for zero order.
These are the units for a first-order rate law.
These are the units for a second-order rate law.
Right: third order overall gives M⁻² s⁻¹.

items.q: For A + B → C, the rate is first order in B. When [A] and [B] are both doubled at the same time, the initial rate becomes 8 times larger. What is the order in A?
options: Zero order
First order
Second order
Third order

why.correct: Doubling [B] alone doubles the rate (first order). The rest of the factor of 8 comes from A: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 = 2², so the order in A is 2.
options: Zero order in A would make the total change only 2.
First order in both would give 2 × 2 = 4, not 8.
Right: 2ᵐ × 2¹ = 8 gives m = 2.
This puts the whole factor of 8 on A and forgets the doubling from B.

items.q: For the rate law rate = k[NO₂]², the concentration of NO₂ is doubled at constant temperature. Predict each change.

variables.name: Initial rate
variables.why: The rate depends on [NO₂]², so doubling [NO₂] multiplies the rate by 4.

variables.name: Rate constant k
variables.why: k depends on temperature and the reaction, not on concentration.

variables.name: Overall order of the reaction
variables.why: The order is a property of the rate law (2 here); it does not change with concentration.

why.correct: The rate goes up by 2² = 4. The rate constant and the order stay the same: k changes only with temperature (or a new pathway).

items.q: Which statements about a rate law are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The rate constant k changes when the temperature changes
The rate constant k changes when a concentration changes
The orders equal the coefficients in the overall balanced equation
The units of k are the same for each rate law

why.correct: k depends on temperature. Changing a concentration changes the rate, not k; orders need not match overall coefficients; and the units of k depend on the overall order.
options: Right: k is a constant at one temperature only.
Concentration changes the rate; k stays the same at a given temperature.
Orders often differ from the overall coefficients; they must be measured.
The units of k depend on the overall order: s⁻¹ for first order, M⁻¹ s⁻¹ for second order.

items.q: A reaction has rate = k[A]² with k = 0.62 M⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the rate, in M/s, when [A] = 0.040 M?

mistakes.why: Value: square the concentration. The rate law is second order in A.
Value: you doubled [A] instead of squaring it. (0.040)² = 0.0016, not 0.080.

items.q: A reaction is zero order in its only reactant. Which statement describes it?
options: Its rate stays the same as the reactant is used
Its rate doubles when the reactant concentration doubles
It does not start until a second reactant is added
Its rate constant has the units s⁻¹

why.correct: Zero order: rate = k[A]⁰ = k. The rate does not depend on [A], so it stays constant until the reactant runs out. k then has the units of a rate, M/s.
options: Right: a zero-order rate is independent of concentration.
That describes a first-order reactant.
Zero order does not mean "does not react"; it means the rate does not depend on [A].
s⁻¹ is the unit of a first-order k; a zero-order k is in M/s.

items.q: A student wants to find the order in B for A + B → products. Which plan would work?
options: Vary [B] while holding [A] and temperature constant; compare initial rates
Run a single trial and read the order from the coefficient of B in the equation
Run trials that change both [A] and [B] together by the same factor
Run trials at several temperatures, keeping the same [A] and [B]

why.correct: To isolate one order, change only that concentration and hold everything else constant. The ratio of initial rates then depends only on [B].
options: Right: one variable at a time.
The coefficient does not give the order; it must be measured.
Changing both at once mixes their effects (unless one order is already known).
Changing temperature changes k, which says nothing about the order in B.
